title: Lying Face Emoji 🤥 Meaning: The Pinocchio Nose Explained
description: The lying face emoji 🤥 has a Pinocchio nose: someone is lying, fibbing or exaggerating. See how it's used to call out others, admit a white lie, and joke around.
summary: 🤥 is a face with a long, grown-out nose, a reference to Pinocchio. It means lying. People use it to accuse someone of not telling the truth, to confess a fib of their own, or to tag a statement as an obvious exaggeration.
meaning: The reference is to Pinocchio, the wooden puppet from Carlo Collodi's Italian novel, whose nose grows when he lies. Thanks largely to the Disney film, the growing nose is understood in much of the world as shorthand for dishonesty. 🤥 puts that image on a smiley, and its meaning is narrower than almost any other face emoji: somebody is not telling the truth.

The most common use is an accusation. Replying 🤥 to “I only had one drink” or “my phone died” says “I don't believe you.” It tends to be lighter than typing “liar,” and between friends it is usually teasing. Aimed at public figures, companies or rival fans, it is harsher, a flat statement that a claim is false.

People also turn it on themselves. “Told my trainer I've been stretching every day 🤥” is a confession of a white lie, shared for laughs. Adding it to your own sentence can mark the sentence itself as untrue, working like a sarcasm tag: “I love waking up at 5 a.m. 🤥” means the opposite.

For all its clarity, 🤥 is not used much. Cap, the slang term for a lie, gave rise to 🧢 as the popular way to call something false, and many people prefer 🤨 or 🙄 to express disbelief. The lying face shows up mostly where the Pinocchio image adds something: playful call-outs, political commentary, and jokes about tall tales.

contexts.label: In texting
contexts.body: It challenges excuses and tall stories, usually with affection. A friend claims they caught a fish “this big” and gets 🤥 back. It also owns up to small deceptions, like telling a host the meal was delicious. With people you do not know well, an accusation of lying can sting even as a joke.

contexts.label: On social media
contexts.body: It appears under statements users consider false: campaign promises, advertising claims, influencer denials, transfer rumors. Fact-check style posts and fan arguments use it as a verdict. Because it calls someone a liar outright, it raises the temperature of a thread more than a skeptical emoji would.

contexts.label: At work
contexts.body: There are few good uses. Suggesting a colleague or client is lying, even playfully, is a serious thing to put in writing. The safe exception is obvious self-mockery, such as “this will only take five minutes 🤥” about your own estimate. Otherwise, raise doubts with words and evidence.

examples.meaning: Quoting someone's claim and calling it untrue; they have clearly not left yet.

examples.text: Told the dentist I floss daily 🤥
You did NOT bench that much 🤥
I'm totally fine with you eating the last cookie 🤥
examples.meaning: Marking the sender's own statement as false; they do mind.

examples.text: Said I was sick but I'm at the beach 🤥

combos.meaning: Doubling up on “that's a lie,” combining Pinocchio with the slang cap.
Pointing at the growing nose; “your lie is showing.”
A fib told with fingers crossed, often an admitted white lie.
Calling someone both dishonest and foolish; a harsh put-down.

confusedWith.difference: 🤨 expresses suspicion: the sender doubts what they heard but has not reached a verdict. 🤥 delivers the verdict and says it is a lie. Use 🤨 to question and 🤥 to accuse or confess.

🤡 calls someone a fool, often for believing something or embarrassing themselves. 🤥 calls them a liar. A person can be wrong and a clown without being dishonest, so the two insults are not interchangeable.
🤐 withholds information by staying silent. 🤥 gives false information. Keeping a secret and telling a lie are different acts, and these emojis mark that line.

avoid: Do not use it when someone tells you about something painful or personal, because doubting them can do real harm.
Avoid aiming it at coworkers or customers, where an accusation of lying has consequences.
Skip it in heated arguments unless you are prepared for the conversation to become about the insult.
design: A yellow face with a long nose jutting out to one side, raised eyebrows and a slightly uneasy or guilty expression. All major platforms draw the Pinocchio nose the same color as the face, not as wood. The nose points left on some designs and right on others, and the mouth varies from a small frown to a nervous half-smile.

faqs.q: Why does the 🤥 emoji have a long nose?
faqs.a: It refers to Pinocchio, the puppet whose nose grows whenever he tells a lie. The story made a long nose a widely recognized symbol of dishonesty, and the emoji borrows it to mean lying.
It can be, since it calls someone a liar. Among friends it is usually a joke about exaggeration or excuses. Directed at strangers or in serious disputes, it is an accusation and will be taken as one.

Both call something a lie. 🧢 comes from the slang “cap” and “no cap” and is the more current, casual choice among younger users. 🤥 is the literal, universally understood version that needs no knowledge of slang.

faqs.q: What does 🤥 mean from a girl or a guy?
faqs.a: Either they think you are fibbing or they are admitting that they did. If it follows your claim, they are teasing or doubting you. If it is attached to their own sentence, they are telling you not to believe it.

faqs.q: When was the lying face emoji added?
faqs.a: 🤥 was approved in 2016, in the same release that brought 🤡, 🤠, 🤤 and 🤢 to emoji keyboards. It has kept the same Pinocchio design ever since.
